lessons.title: Introduction to C++
objectives: Understand what C++ is used for
lessons.content: C++ is a compiled, high-performance language used for operating systems, game engines, and performance-critical software. Every C++ program starts execution from a main() function.
lessons.notes: C++ code must be compiled before it runs — unlike JavaScript, the browser cannot execute it directly.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting the semicolon at the end of a statement, a very common first error.
lessons.practice: Predict the output of the example program before checking it.
lessons.challenge: Change the printed message to include your own name.

hint.en: Used in game engines and operating systems.
hint.sw: Hutumika kwenye game engines na mifumo ya uendeshaji.

explanation.en: C++ is compiled to fast native code.
explanation.sw: C++ hukusanywa kuwa msimbo wa haraka.

quiz.question: Where does a C++ program start executing?

explanation.en: cout sends output to the console.

lessons.title: Variables & Data Types
objectives: Use int, double, char and bool
lessons.content: Unlike Python or JavaScript, C++ requires you to declare a variable's type up front — int for whole numbers, double for decimals, char for a single character, bool for true/false.
lessons.notes: C++ is statically typed: a variable's type cannot change after it's declared.
lessons.mistakes: Assigning a decimal value to an int variable and losing the fractional part silently.
lessons.practice: Declare an int, a double and a bool, then print all three.
lessons.challenge: Declare a char variable holding a single letter and print it.

quiz.question: Unlike Python, C++ requires you to:
options: Declare a variable's type up front

explanation.en: The type is fixed at declaration.

lessons.title: Input & Output
lessons.content: cout sends output to the console using the << operator, while cin reads input from the user using >>, both defined in the iostream header.
lessons.notes: cin >> stops reading at the first whitespace, which matters when reading multiple values.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting #include <iostream> and using namespace std, causing compile errors.
lessons.practice: Read an integer from the user with cin and print it back.
lessons.challenge: Read two numbers and print their sum.

quiz.question: Which reads input from the user?
Which header provides cin and cout?
If a=2 and b=3 are read, what does cout << a + b print?

lessons.title: Operators
lessons.content: C++ supports the standard arithmetic operators. Dividing two integers performs integer division and truncates the decimal part, unlike Python 3's / operator.
lessons.notes: Use static_cast<double>(a) / b when you need a decimal result from integer variables.
lessons.mistakes: Expecting 7 / 2 to equal 3.5 instead of 3 when both operands are ints.
lessons.practice: Divide two int variables and observe the truncated result.
lessons.challenge: Cast one operand to double to get a decimal result instead.
lessons.code:
int a = 7, b = 2;
cout << a / b;

quiz.question: What does int a=7,b=2; cout << a / b; print?

hint.en: At least one operand must be floating-point.

explanation.en: % returns the remainder of integer division.

lessons.title: Conditions
lessons.content: C++ conditionals use if, else if, and else with curly braces defining each block, similar in structure to JavaScript.
lessons.notes: Braces are optional for single-statement blocks but recommended for clarity and to avoid bugs.
lessons.mistakes: Omitting braces on a multi-line block, causing only the first line to be conditional.
lessons.practice: Write an if/else that checks whether a number is positive, negative, or zero.
lessons.challenge: Combine two conditions using && in a single if statement.

quiz.question: What does this print?

explanation.sw: Tawi la kwanza lenye kweli hutekelezwa.

quiz.question: What defines a block in C++?

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.content: C++ for loops declare a counter, a condition, and an increment in one line. while loops repeat as long as a condition stays true.
lessons.notes: An off-by-one error in the loop condition is one of the most common bugs in any language.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting to increment the loop variable in a while loop, causing an infinite loop.
lessons.practice: Use a for loop to print numbers 1 through 5.
lessons.challenge: Rewrite the same loop using while instead of for.

quiz.question: How many numbers does this print?
quiz.code: for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) cout << i << " ";

quiz.question: A while loop repeats:
options: As long as the condition stays true

explanation.en: It stops when the condition is false.

lessons.title: Functions
objectives: Define a function with a return type
lessons.content: C++ functions declare a return type before their name. A function that returns nothing uses void as its return type.
lessons.notes: The function's return type must match what it actually returns, or the compiler will reject it.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting to declare a function before using it earlier in the file.
lessons.practice: Write an int add(int a, int b) function and call it.
lessons.challenge: Write a void function that only prints, without returning a value.

quiz.question: Where is the return type written?
What does add(2,3) print?
quiz.code: int add(int a,int b){ return a+b; }

quiz.question: A function that returns nothing uses:

explanation.sw: void humaanisha hakuna thamani ya kurudisha.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.content: C++ arrays have a fixed size decided at declaration time and are accessed with zero-based indexing, similar to JavaScript and Python arrays/lists.
lessons.notes: C++ does not check array bounds automatically — accessing an out-of-range index is undefined behavior.
lessons.mistakes: Reading or writing past the end of an array without any error being raised.
lessons.practice: Declare an array of 5 ints and print the third element.
lessons.challenge: Loop through the array and print every element.

quiz.question: What is the last valid index of nums[5]?

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.content: The string type from the <string> header provides a safer, more convenient way to work with text than raw character arrays, supporting + concatenation and .length().
lessons.notes: Prefer std::string over C-style char arrays in modern C++ unless you have a specific reason not to.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting #include <string> when using the string type.
lessons.practice: Concatenate a first and last name into a full name string.
lessons.challenge: Print the length of the resulting string.

quiz.question: Which header provides the string type?
What does first + last print for "Wai" and "Tech"?
Which gives the length of s?

explanation.en: length() returns the number of characters.

lessons.title: Structs & Classes Preview
objectives: Group related data with a struct
Preview the difference between struct and class
lessons.content: A struct groups related variables into a single custom type. In C++, struct and class are nearly identical — the main difference is default visibility — and structs are commonly used for simple data bundles.
lessons.notes: Members of a struct are public by default; members of a class are private by default.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting the semicolon after a struct's closing brace, which is required in C++.
lessons.practice: Define a struct Learner with name and level fields.
lessons.challenge: Create a Learner instance and print its fields.

quiz.question: What does a struct do?
options: Groups related variables in one type

quiz.question: How do you access a field?
Main difference between struct and class?

explanation.en: Struct members are public by default.
explanation.sw: Wanachama wa struct ni public kwa chaguo-msingi.

lessons.title: Classes & Encapsulation
objectives: Define a class with private members
lessons.content: Classes bundle data and behavior while controlling access with private and public sections, letting you protect internal state from being changed incorrectly from outside.
lessons.notes: Keeping fields private and exposing controlled methods is the core idea of encapsulation.
lessons.mistakes: Making every member public, which defeats the purpose of encapsulation.
lessons.practice: Define a class BankAccount with a private balance and a public deposit() method.
lessons.challenge: Add a getBalance() method that returns the current balance.

explanation.en: Only the class can touch private data.
explanation.sw: Class pekee inaweza kugusa data ya private.

lessons.title: Vectors
objectives: Use std::vector as a dynamic array
lessons.content: std::vector from the Standard Template Library is a dynamically resizable array, far more flexible than a fixed-size C-style array, and is the default choice for most collections in modern C++.
lessons.notes: vector automatically manages its own memory as it grows, unlike a raw array.
lessons.mistakes: Using a fixed-size array when the number of elements isn't known ahead of time.
lessons.practice: Create a vector<int> and push_back three values onto it.
lessons.challenge: Loop through the vector using a range-based for loop.

explanation.sw: Chaguo la kawaida kwa mikusanyiko mingi.

quiz.question: Which adds an item at the end?
What does for (int n : nums) do?

lessons.title: Maps
lessons.content: std::map stores key-value pairs in sorted order by key, similar in spirit to a Python dictionary or JavaScript object, and is part of the Standard Template Library.
lessons.notes: map keeps keys sorted automatically; unordered_map trades that ordering for faster average lookups.
lessons.mistakes: Accessing a missing key with [] silently inserts a default-constructed value instead of erroring.
lessons.practice: Create a map<string, int> tracking XP per language and insert two entries.
lessons.challenge: Look up one entry and print its value.

explanation.en: The value for key cpp is 40.

quiz.question: Which header is needed for map?

lessons.title: Exception Handling
objectives: Use try/catch to handle runtime errors
lessons.content: C++ exceptions let you signal and handle runtime errors using throw, try and catch, preventing an unexpected condition from crashing the whole program.
lessons.notes: Catching by reference (catch (const exception& e)) avoids unnecessary copies of the exception object.
lessons.mistakes: Throwing raw values instead of proper exception types, losing useful error information.
lessons.practice: Write a function that throws a runtime_error when given a negative number.
lessons.challenge: Wrap a call to that function in a try/catch block.

lessons.title: Pointers & References
lessons.content: A pointer stores the memory address of another variable. A reference is an alias for an existing variable and, unlike a pointer, cannot be reassigned or left null once bound.
lessons.notes: References are generally safer and preferred when reassignment or nullability isn't needed.
lessons.mistakes: Dereferencing a pointer that hasn't been initialized, leading to undefined behavior.
lessons.practice: Declare an int, then a pointer to it, and print the value via the pointer.
lessons.challenge: Declare a reference to the same int and modify the value through the reference.

quiz.question: A pointer stores:
options: The memory address of another variable

explanation.sw: int* ptr = &x ina anwani ya x.

explanation.en: *ptr reads the value at the address.

quiz.question: Compared to a pointer, a reference:
options: Cannot be reassigned or null once bound

explanation.en: It always refers to the same variable.

lessons.title: Smart Pointers
lessons.content: Smart pointers like unique_ptr automatically free memory when they go out of scope, eliminating a huge class of manual memory-management bugs common with raw new/delete.
lessons.notes: unique_ptr cannot be copied, only moved — enforcing single ownership of the resource.
lessons.mistakes: Forgetting to call delete on a raw pointer, causing a memory leak — smart pointers solve exactly this.
lessons.practice: Create a unique_ptr<int> and dereference it to print the value.
lessons.challenge: Explain why unique_ptr can't simply be copied to another variable.

quiz.question: What does unique_ptr do?
options: Frees memory automatically when out of scope

quiz.question: Smart pointers help avoid:
options: Memory leaks and manual delete bugs

lessons.title: Move Semantics Overview
objectives: Understand the cost of unnecessary copies
lessons.content: Move semantics, introduced in C++11, let resources like heap-allocated memory be transferred between objects instead of expensively copied, which is central to how containers like vector perform well.
lessons.notes: std::move doesn't move anything itself — it casts a value to an rvalue reference, enabling the compiler to choose a move instead of a copy.
lessons.mistakes: Assuming std::move() immediately destroys the original object, rather than just enabling a move.
lessons.practice: Research the difference between a copy constructor and a move constructor.
lessons.challenge: Describe, in your own words, why moving a large vector is cheaper than copying it.

quiz.question: After vector b = std::move(a), a is:
options: Destroyed and cannot be named again

explanation.en: a is moved-from and should be reassigned before use.
explanation.sw: a imehamishwa na inapaswa kupewa thamani kabla ya matumizi.
